bib.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
bib.venue: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017)

question: How are existing methods for explaining individual model predictions related, and is there a unique feature-attribution measure with desirable properties?
hypothesis: Shapley values of a conditional expectation function are the unique additive attribution satisfying local accuracy, missingness and consistency, and estimators built on this are more efficient and closer to human intuition than LIME and DeepLIFT.
contributions: Define the class of additive feature attribution methods, unifying six methods
Show Shapley values are the unique solution in the class with three properties, and propose SHAP values
Propose Kernel SHAP, Deep SHAP (and Max SHAP, Linear SHAP, Low-Order SHAP) and show better efficiency and agreement with human intuition

method.summary: Theory unifying LIME, DeepLIFT, LRP and Shapley-based methods as additive feature attribution; derives the Shapley kernel so weighted linear regression recovers Shapley values (Kernel SHAP) and adapts DeepLIFT to Deep SHAP. Evaluated on decision-tree sample efficiency, two MTurk studies and an MNIST convnet.

results.claim: Only one additive feature attribution explanation model satisfies local accuracy, missingness and consistency: the Shapley values.
results.setup: Theoretical; holds for a fixed simplified-input mapping h_x
results.quote: Under Properties 1-3, for a given simpliﬁed input mapping hx, Theorem 1 shows that there is only one possible additive feature attribution method.

results.claim: The class of additive feature attribution methods unifies six existing methods.
results.setup: LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, Quantitative Input Influence
results.quote: The new class uniﬁes six existing methods

results.claim: Methods not based on Shapley values violate local accuracy and/or consistency.
results.setup: Follows from Theorem 1; all Section 2 methods already satisfy missingness
results.quote: This result implies that methods not based on Shapley values violate local accuracy and/or consistency (methods in Section 2 already respect missingness).

results.claim: LIME's heuristic loss, kernel and regularizer do not recover Shapley values, so local accuracy and/or consistency are violated.
results.setup: Linear LIME with LIME's default choices
results.quote: using these choices, Equation 2 does not recover the Shapley values.

results.claim: Kernel SHAP gives more accurate estimates with fewer evaluations of the model than Shapley sampling and LIME, especially with regularization.
results.setup: One input each, decision tree using all 10 features (A) and 3 of 100 features (B); Kernel SHAP with debiased lasso; 10th and 90th percentiles over 200 replicates per sample size; no numeric values given (Fig 3)
results.quote: This leads to more accurate estimates with fewer evaluations of the original model than previous sampling-based estimates of Equation 8, particularly when regularization is added to the linear model (Figure 3).

results.claim: Human explanations in an MTurk study agreed much more with SHAP than with LIME or original DeepLIFT; the sickness-score setting had 30 participants.
results.setup: Sickness score: output 2 when fever and cough both present, 5 when only one, 0 otherwise; most common explanation shown; no significance test or agreement metric reported
results.quote: Human feature impact estimates are shown as the most common explanation given among 30 (A) and 52 (B) random individuals, respectively.

results.claim: The max-allocation human study had 52 participants.
results.setup: Three men, profit equals the maximum questions answered correctly (5, 4, 0 correct, so $5); compared LIME, original DeepLIFT, SHAP
results.quote: Human feature impact estimates are shown as the most common explanation given among 30 (A) and 52 (B) random individuals, respectively.

results.claim: On MNIST, SHAP and LIME were each run with 50k samples; 20% of pixels were masked to switch the predicted class from 8 to 3, with change in log-odds over 20 random images favouring better Shapley approximations.
results.setup: Pre-trained convnet from Shrikumar et al. 2017 (2 conv + 2 dense + 10-way softmax); inputs in [0,1]; Kernel SHAP; LIME with single-pixel segmentation; log-odds values only in a figure
results.quote: SHAP and LIME were both run with 50k samples (Supplementary Figure 1)

results.claim: Linear regression with the Shapley kernel costs O(2^M + M^3), efficient for small M.
results.quote: Since linear regression using Theorem 2 has complexity O(2M + M 3), it is efﬁcient for small values of M
results.note: Text extraction flattens the superscripts: 2^M and M^3

results.claim: Max SHAP computes Shapley values of a max over M inputs in O(M^2) instead of O(M 2^M).
results.setup: Sorted-input permutation formulation; algorithm is in Supplementary Material, not in this PDF
results.quote: lets us compute the Shapley values of a max function with M inputs in O(M 2) time instead of

limits: Uniqueness holds only for a given simplified-input mapping h_x.
Estimators assume feature independence and optionally model linearity (Eq 11, 12); the conditional expectation is approximated.
Evaluation is qualitative: figures only, no numeric accuracy, no significance test, user studies with 30 and 52 people on toy problems; the authors assume human agreement is the right yardstick.
Proofs, Max SHAP algorithm and Supp. Fig 1 are in a supplement not in this PDF.
Authors name faster model-type-specific methods with fewer assumptions and interaction effects as future work.

terms.definition: any interpretable approximation of the original model
have an explanation model that is a linear function of binary variables
the explanation model matches the output of f for the simplified input x' corresponding to x
features missing in the original input have no impact (x'_i = 0 implies phi_i = 0)
if a model changes so that some simplified input's contribution increases or stays the same regardless of the other inputs, that input's attribution should not decrease
the Shapley values of a conditional expectation function of the original model
